name: Yusuf Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior operator on Press 2 at Merrow Aluminium, out past the bypass. We push hot aluminium through a steel die, like toothpaste through a tube, to make the frames for windows and doors. I set the billet temperature and the ram speed, change dies, and watch the profile come out on the run-out table forty metres long. The best moment is a new die running clean first time. The worst is a die that sticks at 500 degrees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else fills your time, outside the press?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a little side business selling refurbished power tools online, which I run with my cousin Omar. I use AI every day for it, writing the listings and answering buyers. At the plant I use it to make sense of our temperature logs. My fiancée Leila is a dental nurse, and we're getting married in the spring, inshallah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be fine. A bit of a shame, because the tools are useful, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that it's just another tool, like a better spreadsheet. To friends I'd say the people who panicked wasted their energy. Online I'd post a few of my listings and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd carry on building. Merrow's busy, and the tool business makes about £400 a month on the side. AI not changing the world doesn't change my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running Press 2, keep the side business growing, and save £300 a month for the wedding and a deposit. I'd look at buying a second-hand bending machine with Omar, so we can start making simple aluminium balustrades for local builders. That's maybe £6,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why balustrades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every new house and balcony round here needs railings, and I know aluminium. Builders tell me the wait is eight weeks. If Omar and I can do it in two, we've got customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, honestly. If they go up, house building slows, and both Merrow and our little business feel it. But that's normal business.

I'd tell friends the people who **panicked** wasted their energy.

AI not changing much doesn't change **my plans**.
do: Save **£300 a month** for the wedding and a deposit.
Buy a **bending machine** with my cousin for about £6,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That sounds about right to me. Office jobs first, robots slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is an opportunity if you're willing to work for it. To friends I'd say nobody's owed a job, so build something. I'd post about the business and maybe help a few friends set up their own listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well. The thinking work in my side business, the listings, quotes and bookkeeping, AI already does for me. That frees me up to do the hands-on fabrication that customers pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the bending machine in the first six months and start the balustrade business properly with Omar. I'd use AI for every quote and invoice. I'd stay at Merrow for a steady wage until the business makes at least £1,500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Merrow, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. Leila and I have a wedding to pay for, and my father always says never jump until you can see the other side. Maybe in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Merrow would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads in the planning office. Some of them have been there twenty years and never touched a computer beyond email. I'd offer to show them a few things, if they'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. And robots that can build and fit by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need to move now, not wait for the government. To friends I'd say families should pull together, pool savings and back each other's businesses. I'd say the same at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think Press 2 is gone by 2031, and so is a lot of fabrication. If robots can bend and weld as well as me, my balustrade plan has three years, not twenty. Leila's job is hands-on too, so we'd both be on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Merrow within a year and put everything into the business, while there are still three years before robots match people. I'd buy a small robot welding cell myself as soon as they're affordable, so I'm the one owning it. And I'd keep six months of money aside, no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but mostly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a robot cell yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots are going to take the work, I'd rather own the robot than compete with it. Same as buying a van instead of walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we keep the wedding small and keep the savings safe. She'd agree, she's more careful than me. And her uncle has a dental practice, so she might be fine longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's a good window for a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when hard workers can get ahead. At work I'd tell people to learn the AI tools and start something on the side. Online I'd keep posting about the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I've got time to build the business properly and get the robots in before everyone else. I'd be a bit worried about big firms moving in, but less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Merrow for two years, then go full-time on the business. I'd buy the bending machine now and a robot cell around 2030. Leila and I would buy a small house in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the big firms do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy up all the robots and undercut small shops like ours. That's my real worry. Not the robots, the big players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on anyone from Merrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they're good. One or two of the lads I trust. A family business works better with people you know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version, and people who work hard will be fine. I'd encourage friends to build businesses. At the mosque I'd say the same: prepare, work, trust God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. Ten years is enough to build a proper business with Omar, own the machines, and have a family. I'd see it more as a chance than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Merrow a few years, grow the business slowly, then go full-time around 2030. Leila and I would buy a house and have children. I'd keep using AI for the business every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy. Thinking there's always time. I'd set myself targets each year and stick to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your children in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they want it. I'd want them to learn a trade first, then decide. Work with your hands, then think about the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's only three years to build before robots catch up. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy machines, and less red tape so we can start quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's what matters. If small family businesses own some of the robots, ordinary people still have a stake.

He'd rather **own robots** than compete with them, and fears big firms most.
